title: Natural selection turns island herbaceous plants into shrubs and trees

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Natural selection turns island herbaceous plants into shrubs and trees

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because trees rarely reach distant oceanic islands, herbaceous plants that colonise them gain an advantage by growing taller, so natural selection often converts insular herbaceous plants first into bushes and then into trees, explaining why islands have trees in orders that are elsewhere herbaceous.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: If so, natural selection would often tend to add to the stature of herbaceous plants when growing on an island, to whatever order they belonged, and thus convert them first into bushes and ultimately into trees.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XII, “Geographical Distribution, continued”; section “On the inhabitants of oceanic islands”. Scope: flowering plants on oceanic islands

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch12-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Repeated evolution of island woodiness is testable with phylogenies and traits. Existing observational data have weaker power to isolate Darwin's particular selective cause from several modern alternatives.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct growth-form evolution in island plant radiations and compare transitions from herbaceous mainland ancestors to woody island descendants with mainland controls. Test whether repeated insular woodiness is associated with selection on height and ecological release from trees.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Woodiness can evolve for drought, longevity, or seasonality rather than competition for height.

Trait coverage is incomplete and some TRY access is conditional.

Ancestral states and colonization direction can be uncertain.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.72
discriminating power: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.58
data existence: 0.84
analysis feasibility: 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Island woodiness relative to mainland relatives is recoverable from trait databases and floras for many clades. Separating colonization by woody lineages from change after arrival needs a tree and is only partly assembled. The adaptive story about stature under selection is an interpretation of that pattern, so the data resolve the comparative prediction more than the mechanism.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare growth form of island endemics with their closest mainland relatives and ask whether shifts from herb to shrub or tree are concentrated on oceanic islands that lacked tree colonists in that clade. Woodiness that arrived already evolved on the mainland would fail the in-situ selection scenario.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Ancestral growth form and sister-species pairs are not stored as one global analysis table.

Woody colonists establishing more easily than herbs imitates evolution of woodiness after arrival.

The selection mechanism is stronger than the woodiness pattern alone.
